system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

=== EXTRACTED CLINICAL ENTITIES — YOU MUST RETAIN ALL OF THESE ===
Patient: male | Age: None
Primary Diagnosis: Bloodstream infection (MRSA) with secondary complications: Infective Endocarditis, Spondylodiscitis, and Ileopsoas Abscess
  Secondary: Bacterial Endocarditis (Mitral Valve)
  Secondary: Pyogenic Spondylodiscitis (L3/L4)
  Secondary: Left Ileopsoas Abscess
  Secondary: Sacral Pressure Injury
  Secondary: Chronic Kidney Disease (on Hemodialysis)
  Secondary: Arteriovenous Fistula Stenosis
  Secondary: Suspected Amyloidosis
Symptoms at admission: Severe left lower back pain; Asthenia (weakness); Altered gait (difficulty walking); Secretion from catheter dressing
Anomalies/Findings:
  [CRITICAL] Blood Culture Positive for Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA) = Positive (OXA R) (normal: Negative)
  [CRITICAL] Vegetation in Mitral Valve = Present (normal: Absent)
  [CRITICAL] Infectious Spondylodiscitis with Anterior Epidural Abscess = L3/L4 level (normal: No infection or abscess)
  [ABNORMAL] Left Ileopsoas Abscess = 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm (normal: No collection)
  [ABNORMAL] Sacral Pressure Injury = Present (normal: Intact skin)
  [ABNORMAL] Arteriovenous Fistula Stenosis = Local stenosis noted (normal: Patent (open) fistula)
  [BORDERLINE] Bibasilar Crackles = Discreet (normal: Clear breath sounds)
  [ABNORMAL] Irregular Heart Rhythm = Present (normal: Regular rhythm)
Procedures performed:
  • Catheter Removal on 11/08/2020
  • Surgical Debridement of Sacral Pressure Injury
  • Attempted Percutaneous Abscess Puncture on 12/02/2020
  • Hemodialysis on Ongoing (Tue, Thu, Sat)
Medications:
  • Vancomycin — Antibiotic to kill the resistant bacteria in the blood and body. | Dosage: 0.5 g after each scheduled hemodialysis session
Warning signs to mention:
  ⚠ Fever or chills
  ⚠ Increased pain in the back or hip
  ⚠ Redness, swelling, or discharge from the dialysis fistula site
  ⚠ Worsening of the sacral wound (smell, increased pain, or pus)
Follow-up appointment: Amyloidosis Cardiology Outpatient Clinic on 01/13/2021
Follow-up appointment: Pressure Injury Surgery Outpatient Clinic on 01/16/2021
Follow-up appointment: Motor Rehabilitation appointment (date to be scheduled by Physiatry)
Follow-up appointment: Phlebography/Ultrasound for Arteriovenous Fistula assessment (date to be scheduled)
Ongoing treatment: Hemodialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays
Ongoing treatment: Vancomycin antibiotic therapy until 01/09/2021
Ongoing treatment: Home care for sacral pressure injury
Hospital stay duration: 1 month 24 days 15 hours
Outcome: alive
=================================================================
CRITICAL RETENTION RULE: Every entity, value, measurement, date, medication name, finding, and recommendation listed above MUST appear in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.
13. CRITICAL — ENTITY RETENTION: Every diagnosis, medication name, procedure, anomaly value, lab result, date, and follow-up instruction listed in the extracted entities block above MUST be explicitly mentioned in your simplified output. Do not omit any of them.

output_text:
Your son, [person], was admitted to the hospital on 11/08/2020 and discharged on 01/02/2021, staying for a total of 1 month, 24 days, and 15 hours. He came in with severe pain in his left lower back, general weakness (asthenia), difficulty walking (altered gait), and fluid leaking from the dressing of his catheter (a tube used for dialysis) in the right femoral vein. The main problem found was a serious infection in the blood (bloodstream infection) caused by a resistant type of bacteria called Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA). This infection spread to other parts of his body, causing infective endocarditis (infection of the heart valve), specifically on the mitral valve, where a clump of bacteria called vegetation was found. It also caused pyogenic spondylodiscitis (infection of the spine and the discs between the bones) at the L3/L4 level, with an abscess (a pocket of pus) in front of the spinal cord called an anterior epidural abscess. Additionally, he had a left ileopsoas abscess, which is a collection of pus in the deep hip muscle, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm. He also developed a sacral pressure injury (a bed sore on the tailbone) due to lying in bed for a long time. His kidneys are not working well (Chronic Kidney Disease), so he needs hemodialysis (a machine that cleans the blood) three times a week. There is also a narrowing (stenosis) in his arteriovenous fistula (the special blood vessel connection used for dialysis) in his left arm. Doctors also suspect he has amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal proteins build up in organs).

During his stay, the catheter was removed on 11/08/2020. He started taking an antibiotic called Vancomycin, which is used to kill the resistant bacteria in his blood and body. The dose is 0.5 g given after each scheduled hemodialysis session. He continues this antibiotic therapy until 01/09/2021. Doctors tried to drain the pus from the hip muscle using a needle (percutaneous abscess puncture) on 12/02/2020, but they could not do it because intestines were in the way. Instead, they treated it with antibiotics. The sacral pressure injury was cleaned surgically (surgical debridement) to remove dead tissue. His blood cultures (tests to check for bacteria in the blood) became negative, meaning the infection in the blood is clearing up. His heart rhythm was irregular, and he had some mild crackles (crackling sounds) when breathing, but he was not in distress.

He will continue hemodialysis on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. He needs to see the Amyloidosis Cardiology Outpatient Clinic on 01/13/2021 to check for the suspected protein buildup. He must attend the Pressure Injury Surgery Outpatient Clinic on 01/16/2021 to check the healing of the bed sore. He also needs a Motor Rehabilitation appointment, which the Physiatry department will schedule. Finally, he needs a Phlebography or Ultrasound to check the narrowing in his dialysis fistula; the date for this will be scheduled by the hospital.

Please watch for these warning signs and contact the doctor immediately if you see them: fever or chills; increased pain in the back or hip; redness, swelling, or discharge from the dialysis fistula site; or worsening of the sacral wound, such as a bad smell, increased pain, or pus. For home care of the sacral wound, please follow the instructions given by the team. The hospital stay is over, and he is alive and stable.
